theory.overview: Transformers revolutionized natural language processing and became the foundation for modern AI like GPT and BERT. Unlike RNNs that process sequences step-by-step, Transformers process entire sequences in parallel using self-attention—each token can directly attend to every other token. This 'attention is all you need' architecture enables massive models that capture complex linguistic patterns and power everything from chatbots to code generation.

sections.title: The Problem with RNNs
sections.content: RNNs process sequences sequentially, which is slow and limits context window. Long-range dependencies (word relationships far apart) are hard to capture due to vanishing gradients. Training is hard to parallelize.

sections.title: Attention: The Core Idea
sections.content: Self-attention allows each position to attend to all positions, computing a weighted sum based on relevance. Think of it as: 'When processing this word, which other words matter most?'
sections.analogy: Like reading a sentence and immediately jumping back to relevant words instead of re-reading sequentially.

sections.title: Query, Key, Value
sections.content: Each input token generates three vectors through learned linear transformations:
sections.computation: Score(i,j) = Query_i · Key_j determines how much position j contributes to position i

sections.title: Multi-Head Attention
sections.content: Multiple attention heads run in parallel, each potentially focusing on different aspects: syntax, semantics, coreference, etc.
mechanism: Split Q, K, V into h heads
Compute attention independently for each head
Each head can learn different relationships
sections.formula: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head_1,...,head_h)W^O where head_i = Attention(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)

sections.title: Positional Encoding
sections.content: Transformers have no inherent notion of position—they need explicit positional information added to inputs.

methods.name: Learned Embeddings
methods.description: Learn position vectors like word embeddings

sections.title: Transformer Architecture
sections.content: The full architecture consists of encoder and decoder stacks with residual connections and layer normalization.

sections.title: Masked Attention (Causal)
sections.content: In decoders (for generation), we prevent positions from attending to future positions. This maintains autoregressive property—each token can only see previous tokens.
sections.implementation: Set attention scores to -∞ for future positions before softmax
sections.purpose: Enable text generation one token at a time

keyConcepts.name: Self-Attention
keyConcepts.description: Each token attends to all other tokens in the same sequence, computing weighted importance.
keyConcepts.complexity: $O(n^2)$ where n = sequence length—quadratic scaling is the bottleneck

keyConcepts.name: Context Window
keyConcepts.description: Maximum sequence length the model can process. Standard: 512-2048 tokens. Long models: 32K-100K+.

keyConcepts.name: Attention Weights
keyConcepts.description: The softmax output showing how much each position contributes to each other position.

keyConcepts.name: Transfer Learning
keyConcepts.description: Pre-train on massive text, fine-tune on specific tasks. Foundation of modern NLP.

complexity.selfAttention: $O(n^2 \cdot d)$—quadratic in sequence length, linear in dimension

practiceProblems.title: Attention Complexity
practiceProblems.description: For sequence length n=512, d_model=768, how many operations in self-attention?
practiceProblems.explanation: Attention computes n×n matrix multiplied by n×d matrix. $512^2 = 262,144$ attention scores, each computed from two d_k=64-dimensional vectors (per head).

practiceProblems.title: Masked Attention
practiceProblems.description: Why does the decoder use masked (causal) attention?
practiceProblems.answer: To prevent positions from attending to future positions, maintaining autoregressive property needed for generation. Without masking, the model could 'cheat' by looking at the answer.
practiceProblems.explanation: In generation, we produce tokens left-to-right. When predicting token t, we can only use tokens 1 to t-1. Masking sets future attention scores to -∞ before softmax.

practiceProblems.title: Multi-Head Purpose
practiceProblems.description: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one larger head?
practiceProblems.answer: Different heads can learn different relationship types: one for syntax, one for coreference, one for semantics, etc. Averaging across diverse perspectives improves representation.
practiceProblems.explanation: Empirically, heads specialize: some attend locally (nearby words), some globally (sentence-wide), some to specific patterns. 8-16 heads common. Ablation: single head hurts performance significantly.

practiceProblems.title: Positional Encoding Necessity
practiceProblems.description: What would happen without positional encoding?
practiceProblems.answer: The model would be permutation-invariant—'The cat sat' and 'cat The sat' would produce identical representations! It couldn't distinguish word order, losing crucial syntactic information.
practiceProblems.explanation: Self-attention alone is position-agnostic: each token's computation is identical regardless of where it appears. Positional encoding injects absolute/relative position information.

practiceProblems.title: Long Sequence Challenge
practiceProblems.description: Design modifications to handle 100,000 token sequences efficiently.
practiceProblems.answer: Solutions: (1) Sparse attention (only attend to nearby + global tokens), (2) Linear attention approximations, (3) Recurrent memory, (4) Hierarchical attention, (5) Sliding window + dilation.
practiceProblems.explanation: Standard attention is $O(n^2)$—untenable at 100K ($10^{10}$ operations!). Sparse patterns reduce to $O(n)$ or $O(n \log n)$. Longformer, BigBird, Performer, FlashAttention are examples.

practiceProblems.title: BERT vs GPT Architecture
practiceProblems.description: Compare BERT (encoder) and GPT (decoder) architectures. Why different choices?
practiceProblems.answer: BERT uses bidirectional encoder—can see all tokens, good for understanding tasks (classification, NER). GPT uses causal decoder—only sees past, good for generation. Different objectives: MLM vs autoregressive.
practiceProblems.explanation: BERT: Masked Language Modeling (predict masked tokens using bidirectional context). GPT: Next token prediction (autoregressive). Encoder-decoder (T5): Best of both for translation/summarization.

codeExample.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import math

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model=512, num_heads=8):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0, "d_model must be divisible by num_heads"
        
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_k = d_model // num_heads  # 64
        
        # Linear projections for Q, K, V
        self.W_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.W_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
    
    def scaled_dot_product_attention(self, Q, K, V, mask=None):
        """
        Q, K, V: (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        Returns: attention output and weights
        """
        scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.d_k)
        # scores: (batch, num_heads, seq_len, seq_len)
        
        if mask is not None:
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)
        
        attn_weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
        output = torch.matmul(attn_weights, V)
        
        return output, attn_weights
    
    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = x.shape
        
        # Linear projections and reshape for multi-head
        Q = self.W_q(x).view(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        K = self.W_k(x).view(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        V = self.W_v(x).view(batch_size, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        # Shape: (batch, num_heads, seq_len, d_k)
        
        # Apply attention
        attn_output, attn_weights = self.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask)
        
        # Concatenate heads
        attn_output = attn_output.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(
            batch_size, seq_len, self.d_model
        )
        
        # Final linear
        output = self.W_o(attn_output)
        return output, attn_weights

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model=512, num_heads=8, d_ff=2048, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, num_heads)
        self.feed_forward = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model)
        )
        
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
    
    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        # Self-attention with residual and norm
        attn_out, _ = self.attention(x, mask)
        x = self.norm1(x + self.dropout(attn_out))
        
        # Feed-forward with residual and norm
        ff_out = self.feed_forward(x)
        x = self.norm2(x + self.dropout(ff_out))
        
        return x

class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model=512, max_len=5000):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Create positional encoding matrix
        pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
        position = torch.arange(0, max_len, dtype=torch.float).unsqueeze(1)
        
        div_term = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * 
                           (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model))
        
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        
        self.register_buffer('pe', pe.unsqueeze(0))
    
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.pe[:, :x.size(1)]

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create sample input
    batch_size = 2
    seq_len = 10
    d_model = 512
    
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_len, d_model)
    
    # Positional encoding
    pos_enc = PositionalEncoding(d_model)
    x = pos_enc(x)
    
    # Transformer block
    transformer = TransformerBlock(d_model, num_heads=8)
    
    # Causal mask for autoregressive generation
    causal_mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len)).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
    
    output = transformer(x, mask=causal_mask)
    
    print(f"Input shape: {x.shape}")
    print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")
    print(f"\nTransformer successfully processed sequence of length {seq_len}")
    
    # Visualize attention
    with torch.no_grad():
        _, attn_weights = transformer.attention(x, causal_mask)
        print(f"\nAttention weights shape: {attn_weights.shape}")
        print(f"  (batch, heads, seq_len, seq_len)")
        print(f"\nFirst head attention for first example:")
        print(attn_weights[0, 0].round(decimals=2))
